cities.base: Center, near the bazaar and the road east to Issyk-Kul, purely a landing and departure buffer
cities.name: Bishkek

cities.base: Town center, walkable to guesthouses and gear rental, base for the traverse and staging point both directions
cities.name: Karakol

places.name: Navat
places.note: Central Asian teahouse, open 10:00 to midnight daily: lagman with veal 475 som ($5.43), samsa 145 som, meat shorpo 385 som on the undated menu. Reviewers say quality varies between Navat branches, so this is the Togolok Moldo 114/1 one.

places.name: Victory Square
places.note: Built in 1985 for the 40th anniversary of the end of WWII: three red granite arcs shaped as a yurt over an eternal flame. Free and always open, a 20 minute stop if you are walking past, not a destination on its own.

places.name: Frunze Museum
places.note: Military museum to the Soviet commander the city was once named after, at 364 Frunze St; 150 som ($1.72), 11:00 to 16:30, closed Mondays. Niche interest only, skip unless you care about Soviet military history.

places.name: Jash Kelin (Osh Plov spot near Jibek Jolu)
places.note: Plov cooked in giant kazans, cheap and filling. Order the plov, nothing else, and eat with the regulars at shared tables.

places.name: Oak Park (Dubovy Park)
places.note: Tree-lined park with Soviet sculptures scattered among the oaks. Quiet, locals walking dogs and playing chess, easy half hour.

places.name: Kyrgyz State Historical Museum
places.note: Reopened after a long renovation: three floors running from prehistory through the nomads and the Soviet years to independence, with the Lenin murals still in place. About 200 som ($2.29), 10:00 to 18:00, closed Mondays; the rainy-afternoon option.

places.name: Ala-Too Square
places.note: The main square, free and open round the clock, with a flag-changing ceremony on the hour that is mildly interesting. Walk through it on the way to the State Historical Museum next door rather than making a trip of it.

places.name: Osh Bazaar
places.note: Sprawling produce and dried fruit market where people actually shop, not a staged version for tourists. Open 09:00 to 18:00 and closed Mondays; come in the morning for dried fruit and nuts to take on the trek.

places.name: CBT Gear Rental
places.note: Rent the tent, sleeping bag and crampons you didn't want to fly with, sort this the afternoon before you start.

places.name: Fat Boys
places.note: The trekker canteen, reliable comfort food and where you'll find a guide or a ride if you need one.

places.name: Karakol Animal Market
places.note: Sunday mornings only, 2 km out of town (taxi about 100 som): farmers trading sheep, cattle and horses, loud and genuinely working. Arrive before 08:00, the livestock part is done by about 10:00, and it smells exactly like you would expect.
places.neighborhood: Outskirts, about 2 km from the centre

places.name: Descent to Altyn Arashan Valley
places.note: Long knee-jarring descent from the lake down into the Altyn Arashan valley, 5 hours or so, dropping through alpine meadow and larch forest. Altyn Arashan itself is a scatter of guesthouses and hot springs at the bottom, a good place to stop for the night rather than pushing straight out to Karakol.

places.name: Karakol Valley Waterfall Walk (low-route alternative)
places.note: The fallback when wind or weather closes the pass. Follows the Karakol river through forest to a waterfall, flat and sheltered by trees most of the way, 3-4 hours round trip. No exposure, no pass, but still gets you into the same valley system.

places.name: Karakol (Fish) Lake side detour
places.note: Skip. A small lake passed early in the standard route, sometimes hyped in trip reports, but it is a muddy pond by comparison to what is coming, and stopping here just burns daylight needed for the pass.

places.name: Moraine Ridge above Ala-Kul Base Camp
places.note: A short scramble up the moraine behind base camp for a sunset view back down the valley, roughly 30 minutes up. Good use of the hour before dark on the acclimatization night if legs have anything left.

places.name: Karakol National Park Entry Checkpoint
places.note: Where park fees are collected before the trail starts, cash only, small entrance building. Not a sight in itself, just where the trek officially begins and where you will queue briefly with other groups on a summer morning.

places.name: Horse and Gear Portage Service (CBT Karakol)
places.note: Arranged through CBT or a Karakol trekking agency, not a fixed place but worth flagging: paying for a horse to carry the heavy pack up to base camp turns day one from a slog into a walk, and buys back energy for the pass. Given the trip is already time-compressed, this is money well spent.

places.name: Ak-Suu (Teploklyuchenka) Guesthouses
places.note: The village at the base of the trailhead, used as a jump-off point rather than a destination. CBT-run guesthouses here can arrange horses to carry gear up to base camp, which is worth paying for given how little time there is to spare.

places.name: Jyrgalan Village
places.note: Skip for this trip. It is a genuinely good base for other treks and has become the community-tourism darling of the region, but it pulls in the opposite direction from Karakol and Ala-Kul, and there is no spare day to reach it. Worth a separate trip, not this one.

places.name: Day 2: Base Camp to Ala-Kul Pass and the Lake
places.note: Steep scree climb from camp to the pass, 2-3 hours, then a short drop to the lake shore. Ala-Kul itself is turquoise, sits at 3560m, ringed by scree slopes with almost no vegetation. Cold and windy at the pass even in summer, go early before afternoon wind and cloud build up.

places.name: Day 1: Ak-Suu Trailhead to Ala-Kul Base Camp
places.note: Trailhead near the Karakol ranger checkpoint past Ak-Suu village, about 18km, 1000m elevation gain, 6-7 hours at a steady pace. Follows the river through forest then opens onto scree and moraine. Most people camp at Ala-Kul base camp around 3200m the night before the pass.

places.name: Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan Traverse (via Ala-Kul Pass)
places.note: The classic traverse, the whole reason to come: Ak-Suu valley to a camp below the pass (6 to 7 hours, 1,000m gain), then the 3,860m pass and the long descent to Altyn Arashan (8 to 9 hours). Snow is normal into June and from October; budget three full days.

places.name: Przhevalsky Museum and Memorial
places.note: Memorial complex by the lake to the Russian explorer, small museum with dated exhibits and limited English. Skip unless it's raining and you've already done everything else on this list, the setting by Issyk-Kul is nicer than the museum itself.

places.name: Yak Bar & Grill
places.note: Sit-down dinner spot in town serving Kyrgyz staples including yak dishes, plov and manty. Good post-trek meal, portions are large, service is slow.

places.name: Ashlyan-Fu Alley
places.note: A canteen alley of Dungan stalls by the Central Bazaar, 08:00 to 20:00 daily, about 200 som ($2.29) a head. Order ashlyan-fu, the cold hot-and-sour noodle soup with starch jelly, usually vegetarian and the thing you will not find elsewhere in the country.

places.name: Fabrika Coffee & Kitchen
places.note: Reliable sit-down breakfast and decent coffee in a town where good espresso is not a given, useful the morning you're packing to head up the valley.

places.name: Karakol Ski Base
places.note: Small ski resort in the valley about 10 km south of the centre; a day lift ticket is $20.58 on the official site. Hours vary, check (the lift may only run Friday to Monday); worth it only if the trek is weathered out and you still want to get up high.

places.name: Central (Bugu) Bazaar
places.note: Everyday town market, useful for stocking up on trail snacks, dried fruit, bread and cheap gear before the trek rather than for sightseeing.

places.name: Holy Trinity Cathedral
places.note: Wooden Orthodox cathedral built without nails after the 1890 earthquake destroyed its predecessor, used for non-religious purposes in Soviet times and a working church again. Free, 08:00 to 17:00 (Sunday from 07:00); 20 minutes, pair it with the Dungan Mosque.

places.name: Dungan Mosque
places.note: Built in 1910 by the Dungan community without nails, Chinese pagoda style rather than dome and minaret; 20 som, photograph it from outside the prayer hall. Hours vary, check: some visitors found it shut on Wednesday mornings. Ten minutes is enough.

places.name: Altyn Arashan Valley and Hot Springs
places.note: Basic wooden tubs fed by a hot spring at the end of the traverse, about 21 km from Karakol in a straight line but much further by road via Ak-Suu and the valley track. Rustic guesthouse-run pools, sometimes cold if a group beat you to it.

places.name: Jeti-Oguz (Seven Bulls) Gorge Walk
places.note: Red conglomerate cliffs, a nature monument since 1975, 40 minutes' drive from Karakol; walk up the valley past Broken Heart rock toward the meadows, 8 to 10 km round trip with little climb. The low-effort day if weather or legs rule out the trek.

places.name: Supara Ethno Complex
places.note: Recreated village with yurts and a big set-menu dinner in the Chunkurchak Gorge, about 27 km south of the centre, so it is a taxi evening, not a city stop. Touristy but the food is good; hours vary, check, and confirm the address when booking.

places.name: Panfilov Park
places.note: Small amusement park with old Soviet rides still running, more about the atmosphere than the rides. Good with jet lag when you do not want to think; ride hours vary, check.

places.name: Faiza
places.note: Cheap canteen-style Kyrgyz cooking with a long lunch queue: lagman 420 som ($4.80), plov 380 som, manty 375 som, samsa 110 som on the undated menu. Open 09:00 to 21:00, Sunday from 10:00.

places.name: Navigator
places.note: Upscale Russian-European place with a patio, live music and breakfast from 08:00 to midnight; borscht 490 som ($5.60), chicken Kyiv 890 som ($10.18), and the average bill runs 1,000 to 2,000 som. Menu prices are dated 4 October, year not shown.

places.name: Dastorkon
places.note: The biggest Dungan, Uyghur and Kyrgyz menu in town, 10:00 to 23:00 daily: ashlyan-fu 185 som ($2.12), Uyghur lagman 425 som ($4.86), manty 345 som, lamb shashlik 595 som ($6.80) on the undated menu.

places.name: Karakol Historical Museum
places.note: In the 1918 to 1920 revolutionary committee building, a museum since 1948: Scythian bronze cauldrons, petroglyphs, felt crafts and 125 Ella Maillart photos, English labels. About 100 som ($1.14), 09:00 to 17:00, but Wanderlog says temporarily closed, so check.

places.name: Tatar Mosque
places.note: Built in 1887 as a mosque and madrasah, the oldest in town, and used as a cinema in Soviet times. A 20 minute stop near the centre; hours vary, check, and check the price at the door.

places.name: Karakol River Park
places.note: Free riverside park on the south side of town, open 08:00 to 20:00, for an easy walk the afternoon before the trek or the day after it.

outings.why: The high point of the trip: a 3900m pass above the turquoise Ala-Kul lake, then a long descent into the Altyn Arashan valley, hard on the knees and weather-exposed above the treeline.
outings.name: Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan traverse, day 1: Karakol to Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan

outings.why: A recovery day after the pass: short walks up the valley and a soak in the mineral hot springs, low effort by design.
outings.name: Altyn Arashan hot springs and valley day
outings.fallback: Just stay at the springs if the legs are done.

outings.why: The exit route back down the valley road, walkable or a rough jeep ride, back to a real bed and a shower in Karakol.
outings.name: Altyn Arashan to Karakol, jeep or walk out

destination.name: Kyrgyzstan
destination.pitch: Real high-mountain trekking without the Nepal crowds, but a 7-day trip is really four and a half usable days once you account for the flights, so pick one trek and do it properly.
destination.caveat: Flying from the US burns almost two full days each way, so a 7-day trip on paper is closer to four and a half usable days on the ground. Put together for you just now from a live search, so check anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.nature: Glacial lakes, a 3900m pass, and alpine valleys with almost no infrastructure between them.
because.adventure: The Ala-Kul to Altyn Arashan traverse is a proper high-pass trek with a night in a valley of hot springs at the end.
because.exploration: Karakol is a launchpad into terrain most travelers never bother reaching.
